the carbon footprint in extensive agroforestry farms is low and it depends on the production system and the species used, with the highest values in dairy sheep farms, followed by the meat production sheep systems.
the low stocking rates and the low quality of the forage in dehesa systems lead to low emissions from the livestock, which are compensated by the carbon sequestration in soils.

the extensive livestock production systems in dehesa have a low carbon footprint due to the low pressure of animals on the territory, which leads to low emissions from enteric fermentation and soil sequestration.

a methodological adjustment to calculate carbon footprint in dehsas, which is essential for the correct comparison with other livestock systems.
the need to develop a carbon footprint methodology adapted to extensive livestock systems, as well as with the importance of taking into account the role of carbon sequestration in the soil.
the study of carbon footprint and carbon compensation in extensive livestock systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
extensive dehesa agrotree systems are a carbon sink and that the extensification process is a carbon neutral process.
extensive systems, such as the dehesa agrosystems, can be considered to be a sustainable option, although they are not the best in terms of carbon footprint.
extensive livestock systems have a low carbon footprint, but they are unable to compete with the more intensive systems in the product unit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the carbon footprint of extensive livestock farms can be considered low if it is referred to the territory, but high if it is referred as product units.
the carbon footprint in dehisas is lower than in other livestock systems, and that this is mainly due to the low stocking rate, the grazing diet of animals and soil sequestration.
the carbon footprint of extensive dehesa agroysstems, in terms of kg of CO 2 eq/ha, is lower than in the intensive livestock systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

extensive systems can be a good carbon footprint option for livestock production, but this should not be understood as a way of compensating for the high environmental impact of the more intensive ones, but rather as a way to mitigate the impact of the latter.
the carbon footprint of livestock systems should not only be referred to the animal but to the territory as a whole, as the carbon sequestration of the soil is a key factor in these systems.

, in order to obtain comparable results, the carbon footprint of livestock systems should not be referred to the product unit but rather to the land area, as this is a more accurate reflection of the environmental pressure exerted by the different livestock systems.
